items.zh: 初禪 · 正明初禪發相
parent: The First Dhyāna: Marks of Realization

zh: 第三、明證初禪相，自有六種：一、名初禪發相；二、明支；三、明因果體用；四、明淺深；五、明進退；六、明功德。第一、正明初禪發相中，復為四意：一、正明初禪發相；二、簡非禪之法；三、釋發因緣；四、分別邪正。第一、初禪發相者，行者於未到地中證十六觸成就，即是初禪發相。云何是證？若行者於未到地中，入定漸深，身心虛寂，不見內外，或經一日乃至七日，或一月乃至一年，若定心不壞，守護增長，於此定中忽覺身心凝然，運運而動，當動之時，還覺漸漸有身，如雲、如影動發，或從上發，或從下發，或從腰發，漸漸遍身。上發多退，下發多進，動觸發時，功德無量。略說十種善法眷屬與動俱起。其十者何？一、定；二、空；三、明淨；四、喜悅；五、樂；六、善心生；七、知見明了；八、無累解脫；九、境界現前；十、心調柔軟。如是十法，與動俱生，名動眷屬勝妙功德莊嚴動法。若具分別，則難可盡，此則略說初動觸相。
en: Third, clarifying the marks of realizing the first dhyāna: this itself has six kinds — naming the first dhyāna's own mark of arising; clarifying its factors; clarifying its cause, effect, substance, and function; clarifying its depth; clarifying its progress and regression; and clarifying its merits.

First, directly clarifying the mark of the first dhyāna's own arising: this, in turn, has four parts — directly clarifying the mark of the first dhyāna arising; distinguishing dharmas that are not truly dhyāna; explaining the causes and conditions of its arising; and distinguishing the deviant from the correct.

First, as for the mark of the first dhyāna's arising: the practitioner, within the "not-yet-arrived" state, realizes the sixteen tactile sensations brought to completion — this is precisely the mark of the first dhyāna's own arising. What is meant by "realizing" this? If the practitioner, within the "not-yet-arrived" state, enters concentration ever more deeply, body and mind empty and still, seeing neither what is within nor without — whether for a single day or as long as seven, whether for a month or as long as a year — and, should the concentrated mind remain unbroken, guarded and protected, growing ever further, then, within this very concentration, one suddenly feels body and mind grow fixed and still, and then set into motion, stirring gradually; and, at the very moment of this stirring, one becomes aware, little by little, of having a body once again, moving and arising like a cloud or a shadow — arising, perhaps, from above, or from below, or from the waist, gradually spreading through the whole body. Arising from above tends, for the most part, toward regression; arising from below tends, for the most part, toward progress. At the very moment this sensation of movement arises, its merit is measureless. In brief, ten kinds of wholesome dharma arise together with it, as its own retinue. What are these ten? Concentration; emptiness; brightness and purity; joy and delight; happiness; the arising of a wholesome mind; clear knowledge and vision; freedom from entanglement and liberation; states manifesting directly before one; and a mind grown pliant and soft. These ten dharmas, arising together with this sensation of movement, are called the retinue of movement — the wondrous, excellent merit that adorns the dharma of movement. Were this to be distinguished in full, it could hardly be exhausted; this, in brief, describes the initial mark of the tactile sensation of movement.

zh: 如是或經一日，或經十日，或一月四月，如是一年，此事既過，復有餘觸次第而發，故名初禪。餘觸發者，謂八觸也：一、動；二、痒；三、涼；四、暖；五、輕；六、重；七、澁；八、滑。復有八觸，謂：一、掉；二、猗；三、冷；四、熱；五、浮；六、沈；七、堅；八、軟。此八觸與前相雖同，而細分別不無小異，更別出名目，足前合為十六觸。此十六種觸發時，悉有善法功德眷屬，如前動觸中說。行者因未到地，發如是等種種諸觸功德善法，故名初禪初發。並是色界清淨四大，依欲界身中而發，故《摩訶衍》云色界四大造色，著欲界身中。問曰：二十七觸何故有去取？復出異觸名料簡（云云）。
en: In this way, whether over the course of a single day, or ten days, or a month, or four months, or even a full year, once this matter has passed, further tactile sensations arise in turn, one after another — hence this is named the first dhyāna. These further sensations that arise are the eight tactile sensations: movement; itching; coolness; warmth; lightness; heaviness; roughness; and smoothness. There are, further, eight more tactile sensations: agitation; pliancy; cold; heat; floating; sinking; firmness; and softness. Although these eight resemble the previous eight in their marks, upon fine distinction they are not without their own small differences, and so are given separate names — together with the first eight, these make sixteen tactile sensations in all.

Whenever these sixteen kinds of tactile sensation arise, each is accompanied by wholesome dharmas and merit as its own retinue, exactly as described above for the sensation of movement. The practitioner, through the "not-yet-arrived" state, brings forth such various tactile sensations, merit, and wholesome dharmas as these — hence this is called the first arising of the first dhyāna. All of this belongs to the pure four elements of the form realm, arising within the body of the desire realm itself — hence the Mahāyāna treatise says that the form derived from the four elements of the form realm attaches itself within the body of the desire realm.
Question: why, among the twenty-seven tactile sensations, are some taken up and others set aside? Further, the names of other, differing sensations are set out and distinguished (and so on).

The eight tactile sensations named here in passing — already used as a shorthand term all the way back in fascicle 3's account of the counting-the-breath wholesome root — turn out to be only half the full picture: a second set of eight (agitation, pliancy, cold, heat, floating, sinking, firmness, softness), close cousins of the first eight but distinguishable on careful attention, complete the full sixteen this section is actually about. The ten-fold retinue of merit accompanying each sensation is the same structure fascicle 3 used for the wholesome-root marks generally — a reminder that these bodily sensations are not incidental side effects of dhyāna but are themselves loaded with the same kind of merit-bearing significance as any other wholesome mark.

items.en: Distinguishing Illness and Demonic Sensations from Genuine Dhyāna

zh: 第二、料簡非禪之相者。問曰：行者於初坐中未得定心，亦發如是冷、暖、動等觸，既無如上所說功德之事，有人言：「此是病法起。」所以者何？如重、澁等，是地大病生；如輕、動觸，是風大病生；如熱、痒等觸，是火大病生；如冷、滑等觸，是水大病生。復次，因暖、熱、痒等，生貪欲蓋；因重、滑、沈等觸，生睡眠蓋；因動、浮、冷等，生掉悔蓋；因強、澁等，生疑蓋；又因重、堅、澁等，生瞋蓋。當知觸等發時，能令四大發病，及生五蓋障法。或言是魔所作，若發動時，如上。過上所說，皆魔觸發，云何以此為初禪耶？答曰：不然。若如汝向所說觸發之相，此是生病生蓋之觸。若如上說及增者，亦是魔觸發相。今說不爾，若未得未到地定，而先發觸者，多是病觸，是生蓋及魔所作。若觸發時，無如上所說十種功德眷屬者，亦是病觸生蓋及魔觸也。今所說觸發者，要因未到地定發，亦具足有諸功德眷屬俱發，故以此為初禪發相，何可疑哉？
en: Second, distinguishing dharmas that are not truly dhyāna. Question: a practitioner, within the very first sitting, before the concentrated mind is even attained, may likewise bring forth such sensations as cold, warmth, or movement, without any of the merit described above being present at all — some say: "This is simply the arising of illness." Why is this? Sensations such as heaviness and roughness arise from an illness of the earth element; sensations such as lightness and movement arise from an illness of the wind element; sensations such as heat and itching arise from an illness of the fire element; and sensations such as cold and smoothness arise from an illness of the water element. Furthermore: warmth, heat, and itching give rise to the hindrance of craving; heaviness, smoothness, and sinking give rise to the hindrance of drowsiness; movement, floating, and cold give rise to the hindrance of restlessness and regret; rigidity and roughness give rise to the hindrance of doubt; and heaviness, firmness, and roughness give rise to the hindrance of anger. One should know that, when such sensations arise, they are able to cause illness to arise within the four elements, and to give rise to the obstructing dharma of the five hindrances as well.

Others say this is the work of a demon: when such sensations arise, those that are as described above are as already explained, but whatever goes beyond what was described above is all a demon's own sensation arising — how, then, could this possibly be taken as the first dhyāna? Answer: this does not follow. If the mark of the sensation's arising is exactly as you have just described, this is a sensation that gives rise to illness and to the hindrances. If it is exactly as described above, and even intensifies beyond it, this too is the mark of a demon's sensation arising. What is being described here, however, is not this: if, before the "not-yet-arrived" concentration is even attained, a sensation arises first, this is, for the most part, an illness-sensation, or one that gives rise to the hindrances, or one that is the demon's own work. And if, when a sensation arises, none of the ten kinds of merit described above is present as its retinue, this too is an illness-sensation, hindrance-arising, or demon-sensation. What is described here as the sensation's arising, however, necessarily arises through the "not-yet-arrived" concentration, and is necessarily accompanied by every one of these merits as its retinue, arising together with it — hence this alone is taken as the mark of the first dhyāna's own arising. What room, then, is there for doubt?

zh: 問曰：未到地前發觸，但是生病生蓋及魔觸，亦有治病除蓋非魔觸不？答曰：亦有此義。問曰：若爾，與初禪觸復云何異？答曰：有異。欲界雖有治病除蓋及非魔觸，而非初禪觸者，此猶是欲界中四大色法，不能發定，無諸功德支林善法，故不名初禪。此則略出欲界善、不善觸相，但行人初坐，或有證此一兩，或都不證。然既有此法，故略出之耳。問曰：未到地中亦發欲界善、不善觸不？答曰：非無此義。
en: Question: if a sensation arises before the "not-yet-arrived" state, is this always simply the arising of illness, the hindrances, or a demon's work — or is there also a sensation that treats illness and removes the hindrances without being the work of any demon? Answer: yes, this sense holds as well. Question: if this is so, how does it differ from the first dhyāna's own sensation? Answer: it does differ. Although the desire realm may have sensations that treat illness and remove the hindrances without being the work of any demon, these are still not the first dhyāna's own sensations — they remain simply the four elements' own material dharma within the desire realm, unable to bring forth concentration, without any of the wholesome dharma of a grove of factors present — hence they are not named the first dhyāna. This, in brief, sets out the marks of wholesome and unwholesome sensation within the desire realm; it is simply that, in a practitioner's very first sitting, one or two of these may sometimes be realized, or none at all may be realized. Since this dharma does exist, however, it is given here in brief. Question: does the "not-yet-arrived" state, too, give rise to the desire realm's own wholesome and unwholesome sensations? Answer: yes, this sense is not absent there either.

This Q&A sharpens the diagnostic criterion from fascicle 3 into something almost clinical: the same eight sensations (cold, warmth, movement, and the rest) can indicate illness, demonic interference, ordinary desire-realm sensation, or genuine dhyāna, and the deciding factor is never the sensation's own quality but strictly its context — whether it arises before or only after the "not-yet-arrived" concentration is actually attained, and whether the full ten-fold retinue of merit accompanies it. A sensation identical in every describable respect can be either meaningless or the mark of a major attainment depending entirely on what came before it — a caution against ever diagnosing a state from its content in isolation.

items.en: Causes and Conditions of Dhyāna's Arising
parent: The First Dhyāna: Marks of Realization

zh: 三、明禪發因緣有二：一者、從初修禪以來，不計勤苦，既有善心，功力成就，自然感報，如《法華》中說：「隨功賞賜，乃至禪定、根、力等事。」復次，有師言：「是十善相應。」此意難見。二者、色界五陰住在欲界身中，麁細相違，故有掉、動八觸等事。譬如世人憂愁煩惱，內起結滯，壅塞不通，令四大受諸熱惱，從心而生，乃至得病至死，不從外來而有苦也。今此禪中有觸樂之事，亦從心有，由數息故，使心軟細，修諸定法，色界定法住在欲界身中，色定之法與欲界報身相觸，故有十六觸次第而生，亦不從外來而能覺知，故名為觸。
en: Third, clarifying that dhyāna's arising has two causes and conditions.

First: from the very outset of cultivating dhyāna, without regard for toil or hardship, once a wholesome mind and the power of one's own effort come to completion, the result is naturally brought about of itself — as the Lotus Sūtra says: "Rewards bestowed according to merit, extending even to dhyāna-concentration, the faculties, the powers, and such matters." Furthermore, one master says: "This corresponds to the ten wholesome actions" — though this sense is difficult to see clearly.

Second: the five aggregates of the form realm come to dwell within the body of the desire realm, coarse and fine at odds with one another, and so such matters as the sensations of agitation, movement, and the rest arise. It is like a person in the world whose sorrow and vexation give rise to an inward knot or blockage, obstructed and unable to flow freely, causing the four elements to suffer their own feverish distress — arising from the mind itself, even to the point of falling ill and dying from it, a suffering that never comes from outside at all. Here, in this dhyāna, the matter of tactile joy is exactly the same, arising from the mind as well: through counting the breath, the mind is made soft and fine, and, as the various dharmas of concentration are cultivated, the concentration-dharma of the form realm, dwelling within the body of the desire realm, comes into contact with the desire realm's own retributive body — hence the sixteen tactile sensations arise, one after another, in sequence, likewise never coming from outside, yet still able to be felt; hence they are named "tactile sensations."

zh: 此八雖有十六，並約四大而發，因四大生：地中四者，重、沈、堅、澁；水中四者，涼、冷、軟、滑；火中四者，暖、熱、猗、痒；風中四者，動、掉、輕、浮。故《金光明》云：「地水二蛇，其性沈下；風火二蛇，性輕上昇。」問：若因四大，但應有四，何得十六？答曰：相兼故得爾。如熱是火體，兼水故有暖，兼風故有痒，兼地故有猗，兼三之時，失本熱相，故說有四。餘三大各兼三義，類此可知。復次，此十六觸各有十種功德善法，合則有一百六十法，而初坐發法之人未必發盡，或發三五，故略出之。問曰：此八觸為當發有次第？為無次第？諸觸之中，先發何等？答曰：若論其次第，亦無定前後。雖四大因緣合時，強者先發，而多見有人從動而發，事如前釋。四者、辨邪正之相，具如前內方便中驗善惡根性相明虛實中說，是中應廣分別。
en: Although these are eight in one counting and sixteen in another, all of them arise with reference to the four elements, born from the four elements themselves: within earth, four — heaviness, sinking, firmness, and roughness; within water, four — coolness, cold, softness, and smoothness; within fire, four — warmth, heat, pliancy, and itching; within wind, four — movement, agitation, lightness, and floating. Hence the Golden Light Sūtra says: "The two serpents of earth and water are sinking by nature; the two serpents of wind and fire are light and rising by nature."

Question: if these arise from the four elements, there should be only four of them — how can there be sixteen? Answer: this comes about through their combining with one another. Heat, for instance, is the very substance of fire; combined with water, it gives warmth; combined with wind, it gives itching; combined with earth, it gives pliancy — and, whenever it is combined with any of these three, it loses its own original mark of heat; hence four are spoken of. Each of the remaining three elements likewise combines with the other three in the same way, and may be understood by this same pattern. Furthermore: each of these sixteen tactile sensations carries its own ten kinds of wholesome, meritorious dharma, which, combined together, come to one hundred sixty dharmas in all — though a person, in the very first sitting where this dharma arises, need not bring forth every one of them; some bring forth only three or five. This, in brief, is set out here.

Question: do these eight — or sixteen — tactile sensations arise in a fixed sequence, or not? Among the various sensations, which arises first? Answer: discussing their sequence, there is, in fact, no fixed order beforehand. Although, when the causes and conditions of the four elements come together, whichever is strongest tends to arise first, it is nonetheless most commonly observed that people's sensations arise beginning with movement, exactly as already explained above. Fourth, distinguishing the marks of the deviant and the correct: this is given in full already, within the internal expedient means, in the discussion of verifying wholesome and unwholesome capacity's clarification of the genuine and the false; this should be distinguished at length here.

The comparison to psychosomatic illness is a genuinely striking move — the treatise explicitly likens the tactile sensations of dhyāna to how ordinary grief and vexation can produce real bodily suffering "arising from the mind itself... never coming from outside at all," using a recognizable everyday phenomenon to make a subtle claim about dhyāna's own sensations plausible. The combinatorial explanation of how four elements produce sixteen sensations (each element's own quality plus its three possible combinations with the others) is a small piece of genuine systematic reasoning embedded in what could otherwise read as simple enumeration — heat combined with water gives warmth, with wind gives itching, with earth gives pliancy, and, in each such combination, the original quality loses its own pure mark of heat.

quiz.q: When the sensation of movement arises, what tends to follow if it arises from above or from below?
options: from above tends to regression; from below tends to progress
quiz.why: "Arising, perhaps, from above, or from below, or from the waist, gradually spreading through the whole body. Arising from above tends, for the most part, toward regression; arising from below tends, for the most part, toward progress."

quiz.q: Which set belongs to the ten wholesome dharmas arising with the sensation of movement?
options: concentration, emptiness, brightness and purity, joy and delight, happiness
quiz.why: "What are these ten? Concentration; emptiness; brightness and purity; joy and delight; happiness; the arising of a wholesome mind; clear knowledge and vision; freedom from entanglement and liberation; states manifesting directly before one; and a mind grown pliant and soft."

quiz.q: Which are the first set of eight tactile sensations?
options: movement, itching, coolness, warmth, lightness, heaviness, roughness, smoothness
quiz.why: "The eight tactile sensations: movement; itching; coolness; warmth; lightness; heaviness; roughness; and smoothness. There are, further, eight more tactile sensations: agitation; pliancy; cold; heat; floating; sinking; firmness; and softness." Together they make sixteen.

quiz.q: What kind of dharma are the first dhyāna's sixteen sensations, and in what do they arise?
options: the pure four elements of the form realm, arising within the desire-realm body
desire-realm elements in a form-realm body
quiz.why: "All of this belongs to the pure four elements of the form realm, arising within the body of the desire realm itself — hence the Mahāyāna treatise says that the form derived from the four elements of the form realm attaches itself within the body of the desire realm."

quiz.q: Clarifying the realization of the first dhyāna has which six parts?
options: arising, factors, cause-effect-substance-function, depth, progress and regression, merits
quiz.why: "Clarifying the marks of realizing the first dhyāna: this itself has six kinds — naming the first dhyāna's own mark of arising; clarifying its factors; clarifying its cause, effect, substance, and function; clarifying its depth; clarifying its progress and regression; and clarifying its merits."

quiz.q: How does the text distinguish the genuine first-dhyāna sensation from those of illness or demons?
options: sensations before the not-yet-arrived state, or without the ten merits, are illness, hindrance, or demonic; the genuine one arises through that state with its merits
quiz.why: "If, before the 'not-yet-arrived' concentration is even attained, a sensation arises first, this is, for the most part, an illness-sensation ... And if, when a sensation arises, none of the ten kinds of merit described above is present as its retinue, this too is an illness-sensation ... What is described here as the sensation's arising, however, necessarily arises through the 'not-yet-arrived' concentration."

quiz.q: Someone says the sensations are illness arising from the elements. Which pairing is part of that claim?
options: heaviness and roughness from earth; lightness and movement from wind; heat and itching from fire; cold and smoothness from water
quiz.why: "Sensations such as heaviness and roughness arise from an illness of the earth element; sensations such as lightness and movement arise from an illness of the wind element; sensations such as heat and itching arise from an illness of the fire element; and sensations such as cold and smoothness arise from an illness of the water element."

quiz.q: The desire realm also has sensations that treat illness and remove hindrances. Why are they not first-dhyāna sensations?
options: they remain the desire realm's material elements, unable to bring forth concentration, without the grove of factors
quiz.why: "Although the desire realm may have sensations that treat illness and remove the hindrances without being the work of any demon, these are still not the first dhyāna's own sensations — they remain simply the four elements' own material dharma within the desire realm, unable to bring forth concentration, without any of the wholesome dharma of a grove of factors present."

quiz.q: In the second cause of dhyāna's arising, how does the text explain where the sensations come from?
options: the form realm's aggregates dwell in the desire-realm body, coarse and fine at odds; the form-realm concentration touches the desire-realm body, not from outside
quiz.why: "The five aggregates of the form realm come to dwell within the body of the desire realm, coarse and fine at odds with one another, and so such matters as the sensations of agitation, movement, and the rest arise ... the concentration-dharma of the form realm ... comes into contact with the desire realm's own retributive body — hence the sixteen tactile sensations arise ... likewise never coming from outside."

quiz.q: Matching the sixteen sensations to the elements, which four belong to fire?
quiz.why: "Within earth, four — heaviness, sinking, firmness, and roughness; within water, four — coolness, cold, softness, and smoothness; within fire, four — warmth, heat, pliancy, and itching; within wind, four — movement, agitation, lightness, and floating."

quiz.q: If the sensations come from four elements, why are there sixteen?
options: through combination: heat is fire's substance; with water it gives warmth, with wind itching, with earth pliancy
quiz.why: "This comes about through their combining with one another. Heat, for instance, is the very substance of fire; combined with water, it gives warmth; combined with wind, it gives itching; combined with earth, it gives pliancy."

quiz.q: Each of the sixteen sensations has ten merits. How many in total, and does a beginner bring forth all?
options: 160 in all; a beginner need not bring forth all, perhaps three or five
quiz.why: "Each of these sixteen tactile sensations carries its own ten kinds of wholesome, meritorious dharma, which, combined together, come to one hundred sixty dharmas in all — though a person, in the very first sitting where this dharma arises, need not bring forth every one of them; some bring forth only three or five."
